#8895. The Benefits of Biking for Seniors, Including the Mental and Physical Payoffs

You might find a few surprising advantages of cycling on this list.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

We know you think we’re going to tell you all the ways cycling improves your heart health and muscle strength—and it does, but guess what? According to a 2023 scoping review in Frontiers in Sports and Active Living, studies show that when older adults cycle regularly, their happiness improves and they are better able to maintain their quality of life.

In fact, even though many people associate aging with physical and mental declines, regular exercise—like a daily bike ride—can help slow or even reverse some of these effects.

“Regular physical activity helps seniors maintain good health, improve their quality of life, and increase their overall well-being,” Mary Sabat, MS, RDN, a personal trainer and dietitian in Georgia tells Bicycling. “It can enhance physical strength, flexibility, and endurance, making it easier to perform daily activities and maintain independence.”

Those are just few reasons why biking for seniors is so great—but here are all the advantages you gain when you start pedaling regularly.

While almost forms of physical activity improve physical and mental health, cycling is particularly well-suited for those in their golden years due to its accessibility. After all, cycling is easy on the joints, even for those with joint pain or injuries. “It can be tailored to individual fitness levels and adjusted to accommodate different abilities and physical limitations, too,” says Sabat. “Recumbent bikes, trikes, or electric-assist bicycles can be used to make cycling more accessible for those with mobility challenges or balance issues.”

Robert Patterson, a cyclist and lawyer, has been cycling for more than 40 years. He points out all the obvious aerobic and strength-building gains he’s enjoyed over the years, but also the psychological benefits. “Cycling also benefits my mental health. My attitude and overall focus are always improved by being on the bike,” he says.

Here are nine reasons, according to the experts, for you to saddle up and hit the road (or the gym) for a ride.

Aerobic exercise is the key to managing heart health. Because the heart is a muscle, it needs to be exercised on a regular basis to maintain its strength and optimal function. And because the heart and lungs work together with the venous system to deliver oxygenated blood to your muscles, any exercise that increases your heart rate and breath rate for an extended period of time will help improve your heart health and overall cardiovascular function.

Plus, as anyone who has ever pushed the pedals and pumped through a 20- or 30-minute bike ride knows, cycling will definitely get your heart rate up. The repetitive cycling motion qualifies as a moderate to intense form of aerobic exercise that you can easily adapt to your personal fitness level. This means that even if you haven’t exercised in years, by starting at a lower intensity and making adjustments to your workouts based on your heart rate, you can safely and effectively add cycling to your weekly routine.

“As individuals age, the risk of heart disease increases,” says Sabat. “Cycling is a low-impact aerobic exercise that helps improve cardiovascular fitness, strengthens the heart muscle, and enhances blood circulation. It can lower the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and high blood pressure, thereby promoting a healthy heart.”

In fact, a series of two 2019 review studies (part 1 and part 2) published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine found that all forms of cycling reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and also reduced the risk factor profile for poor heart health—meaning that cyclists had better body composition stats, blood lipid profiles, cardiorespiratory fitness levels, and more time spent exercising. All of these together help mitigate the risk for developing heart disease.

You can combat practically any chronic condition, including heart disease, along with type 2 diabetes, arthritis, and cancer with a regular ride. Exercise helps keep the blood flowing, systems moving, and cells turning over in a way that promotes overall health. For instance, high-intensity exercise (and high-intensity cycling, specifically) helps improve blood glucose response, according to research, which may reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes.

Even in the case of cancer, participating in a regular cycling routine has been shown to reduce the risk. For example, May 2020 study published in The Lancet found an association between participating in a daily bike commute and a 16 percent decrease in cancer mortality and an 11 percent decrease in cancer incidence.

“By incorporating a ride here and there into their routine, seniors can reduce the risk of chronic conditions. These conditions can be debilitating, but with regular exercise, seniors can take proactive steps toward prevention and management,” Josh Weight, a certified sports physiotherapist and the director of Gravity Physio in Australia tells Bicycling.

It’s not unusual for seniors to experience regular joint pain associated with arthritis or previous injuries. In fact, according to the National Poll on Healthy Aging, about 70 percent of older adults report current joint pain. This can be exacerbated by extended periods spent sitting, or simply not moving around much, as sedentary behavior is directly associated with increased incidences of knee and other joint pain.

While on the surface this may not seem like a big deal, it can lead to a cascading series of events where joint pain or arthritis contributes to a reduced range of motion. This reduced range of motion can influence balance, coordination, and even the ability to perform everyday tasks. These issues can also contribute to a reduced quality of life and even an increased risk of falls. As such, any activity that can be done without contributing to joint pain while protecting and strengthening the structures that help stabilize the joints (muscles, tendons, and ligaments) is an important undertaking for older adults’ overall health and well-being.

“Cycling is a low-impact activity that puts minimal stress on the joints, making it an excellent option for individuals with joint-related issues. It provides a cardiovascular workout without placing excessive strain on the knees, hips, or ankles,” Sabat says.

Whether done on an indoor bike or a more traditional road or mountain bike, one thing’s for sure: Cycling works the legs. It takes muscular strength, power, and endurance to keep the pedals moving, especially when climbing a hill or ramping up the resistance. But it’s not just the legs and glutes that benefit—cycling can help build strength in the shoulders, upper back, and core, as well.

Of course, you may not be looking to build massive quads as one of your long-term fitness goals, but developing muscular strength isn’t just about looking strong—it’s about maintaining your quality of life.

Research estimates muscle mass begins to decline by 3 to 8 percent every decade following your 30th birthday, with those rates increasing further once you hit 60. This age-related muscular decline over time makes it more challenging to continue doing everyday activities like climbing stairs or carrying groceries. It’s important to participate in exercises, like cycling, that will help maintain or build muscle mass over time to safeguard your ability to perform these daily activities.

In fact, according to a 2015 review study published in the European Review of Aging and Physical Activity, adults over 70 years of age experienced increased muscular strength and power when participating in a cycling exercise program at least three times a week for 12 to 16 weeks. This data flies in the face of anyone who believes they can’t develop muscle or strength as they age—it’s not only possible, it’s critical to overall health and functional ability.

One area in which cycling can be particularly beneficial is balance and coordination. This has ties to muscular strength, as strong, trained muscles tend to perform and react more quickly to stimuli than those that aren’t worked regularly. However, it also has to do with the unique requirements of cycling itself.

“Cycling requires balance and coordination to stay upright and navigate,” says Andrew White, a personal trainer and owner of Garage Gym Pro. “This can be especially beneficial for seniors as these abilities tend to decline with age, increasing the risk of falls and injuries.”

This isn’t just conjecture—a 2018 prospective study published in the Journal of Aging and Physical Activity found that older adults (between the ages of 65 and 85) who cycled daily had better balance, a faster pace while walking, and better self-reported lower-extremity function compared to those who didn’t bike regularly. Based on this study, it appears that cycling helps preserve balance and coordination which contributes to lower-body function that can help prevent falls.

Just as muscle mass tends to decline with age, an associated change in body composition takes place, which often leads to increased weight gain. And as weight creeps up, so do the risks for heart disease and chronic illness, particularly in populations considered obese.

Cycling and other forms of exercise can help keep weight and other disease risk factors in check. This is partly due to the muscle-protective benefits exercise offers, but also due to the increased calorie burn that occurs during moderate- to high-intensity exercise like cycling.

“Cycling can help seniors maintain a healthy body weight, reduce excess body fat, and prevent obesity-related health issues,” Sabat emphasizes.

It’s not unusual for seniors to experience social isolation that can contribute to physical and mental health decline. Changes in health, mobility, or driving status can keep seniors alone at home. This is unfortunate because strong social connections are positively associated with longevity.

Cycling can provide seniors with an accessible way to get out and about, and to also engage with other people of all ages. “Cycling can be an enjoyable and social activity for seniors. Exploring outdoor trails, participating in group rides, or engaging in community cycling events can foster a sense of camaraderie and connection with others,” says Weight.

And for seniors who want to start cycling, but don’t know how, community cycling clubs offer a great way to learn and connect at the same time.

In addition to the benefits of social interaction, cycling can boost mental health in a number of ways, especially if you’re riding your bike outside. “Cycling outdoors provides an opportunity to connect with nature, which can be therapeutic and stress-relieving,” says White.

In fact, according to a 2022 study published in the Journal of Affective Disorders, individuals who participated in outdoor cycling (or other outdoor activities like walking, jogging, or team sports), were less likely to experience depression than those who were inactive. Likewise, there’s evidence that even a single outdoor exercise session (like cycling) can impact mood, more than indoor exercise equivalents.

Even in the absence of an outdoor setting, physical activity as a whole is good for mental health. “Regular exercise releases endorphins which can elevate mood and reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression,” Sabat explains.

One final benefit of cycling for seniors: It can support cognitive function. “Studies have shown that physical activity can have positive effects on cognition and may help reduce the risk of cognitive decline and dementia in older adults. Exercise promotes better blood flow to the brain, stimulates the release of hormones that support brain health, and improves memory and attention,” Sabat shares.

Laura Williams, M.S., ACSM EP-C holds a master's degree in exercise and sport science and is a certified exercise physiologist through the American College of Sports Medicine. #8892. The 3 Types of Running Workouts You Need to Train for Your First Half Marathon

These key weekly sessions will carry you to the finish line.

Nowhere in any running rulebook does it say you have to train for a 5K or 10K before signing up for a half marathon. As a beginner, 13.1 miles is an awesome way to approach long-distance running. You just need a plan that meets you where you’re at right now and progresses gradually to get you to the starting line feeling strong.

Cut to Runner’s World’s 20-week beginner half marathon plan created by Meg Takacs, CPT, a UESCA-certified running coach and founder of the Movement and Miles app.

It balances three key workouts designed to help you build endurance safely, recover well, and get comfortable with longer distances. You’ll spread these workouts throughout 20 weeks, which gives you plenty of time to build rather than your typical 10- or 14-week plan.

Each workout progresses as you move through the plan, so it’s a good idea to familiarize yourself with their basic structure and purpose before you jump into training. Here’s how to get the most out of each workout.

Run/walks help you build aerobic fitness and endurance gradually. You’ll start with a one-minute run followed by a one-minute walk for 20 minutes total, adding one minute to the run interval every session. With run/walks starting at three times a week, you’ll work up to a 10-mile run/walk in week 16, where you run for 20-minute intervals and walk for two minutes (this is your weekend long run).

Do the run intervals at a comfortable, low-intensity pace, meaning you should be able to hold a conversation with a friend the whole time. On a scale of 1 to 10 for rate of perceived exertion (RPE), aim for a 2 to 4 for effort level, with 1 being easy like a walk and 10 meaning all-out effort.

Why it works: This is the backbone of the beginner half marathon plan. Run/walk sessions help you build the endurance you need to run farther.

10 x 1 minute walk, 1 minute easy-effort run

In week four of this plan, you’ll start incorporating continuous easy runs, beginning with 25 minutes at a truly easy effort. The longest continuous run you will complete is 8 miles with as few walk breaks as possible by week 17.

Throughout the plan, there’s more of a focus on time-based easy runs rather than distance. “For beginners, time on your feet is more important than mileage in order to get your body gradually acclimated to running,” Takacs previously told Runner’s World.

Why it works: Continuous easy runs help boost endurance and give you the confidence you need to run farther.

Run 25 minutes at an easy effort (RPE 2 to 4), limiting walk breaks as much as possible.

The first of your weekly speed workouts begins in week 3. You’ll complete 400-meter repeats at a moderate effort with two-minute walks in between. Moderate effort is slightly above your easy effort, reaching a 4 to 6 out of 10 RPE. “The goal is to try and run each repeat faster than the last,” Takacs adds.

You should still be able to speak during the work intervals, but you’re breathing heavier and can only talk in phrases. Over the course of the training plan, you’ll work your way up to longer intervals, like 800-meter, 1200-meter, and mile repeats.

Why it works: Speed workouts aren’t just there to help you get faster; they also boost your overall fitness and running economy so easy runs feel easier.

Short postrun strides help build speed and leg turnover, and you’ll find them sprinkled throughout your plan. These accelerations will help you build more speed, improve your running form by getting your legs to turn over quicker, and boost your confidence.

The goal of strides is to run at a hard effort for 10 to 15 seconds, but it doesn’t have to be an all-out sprint. Aim for a 7 to 10 RPE; you should only be able to say a word or three at a time.

In any training plan, strength workouts are crucial to prevent injury, support your running economy and durability, and get stronger. In this plan, you’ll complete strength workouts once or twice a week before or after your runs. Depending on your preference, you can decide to run in the morning, then follow with strength in the afternoon or evening (or vice versa).

Takacs recommends starting with bodyweight exercises if you’re new to strength training and then adding in weights as you get stronger.

There’s a reason coaches tell runners to work hard and recover harder. Your recovery days are meant to feel like a true recovery where you can come back to your next run feeling refreshed, strong, and excited to get back out there.

It’s a good idea to loosen stiff muscles with foam rolling, stretching, and some mobility drills. If you need a complete day off, it’s also okay to not do anything at all except watch TV, read a book, or hang out with friends. A day off is good for the mind and the body. This is also a good opportunity to make sure you’re getting to bed early so you can show up to each run as your best, well-rested self.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and currently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

#8891. Our Editors Ride-Tested Virginia Tech’s Top-Rated Road and Gravel Helmets—Including a $60 Pick That Punches Way Above Its Price

Lab safety scores matter, but so do fit, ventilation, and price. Here’s how the top lids compare.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

As a cyclist for over three decades, I’ve crashed many times. Unfortunately, I’ve also had a few concussions. Because of this, safety is important to me when I choose a new helmet. Over the last few seasons, I’ve tested dozens of great helmets, from budget picks under $50 to go-fast aero lids and lightweight models for over $500. Plus, I also test trail helmets, commuter lids, and everything in between.

When shopping for new road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort. Depending on our riding goals and budget, we also balance weight, aerodynamics, and style. We want safety features, but many riders assume most helmets do a decent job of protecting our noggin—they’re all certified, right?

Helmet safety isn’t as straightforward as it may seem. Current Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) standards—as well as more rigorous, voluntary requirements, such as those from ASTM—account for straight-line impacts and G-forces from a collision. These standards don’t address the rotational forces from a crash that contribute significantly to concussions and traumatic brain injuries. Plus, the CPSC’s standards took effect on March 10, 1999—advancements in technology, design, materials, and manufacturing over the last 27 years have changed bike helmets.

So, what standards and certifications cover rotational forces? Currently, none. To better protect against rotational forces and reduce concussions, many brands incorporate Mips liners (and similar anti-rotational designs) into their helmets. Brands also test their helmets internally to their own, generally unpublished, criteria. The Virginia Tech helmet lab’s STAR score provides the best independent testing and ranking for helmets across most cycling disciplines.

Virginia Tech tests helmets for safety; it doesn’t evaluate fit, comfort, weight, price, or overall practicality. Bicycling’s test team collectively rides tens of thousands of miles each year on tarmac, gravel roads, singletrack, and commuting. That means we have a lot of time to ride-test lids—including more than half of Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR-rated road helmets.

For 15 years, Virginia Tech has tested helmets through a battery of 24 impact tests that analyse safety performance and assign an overall STAR (Summation of Tests for the Analysis of Risk) score.

“The overall score estimates the number of concussions the average person would see if they experienced identical impacts at rates matching their weightings while cycling,” says Virginia Tech’s lab. The lower the STAR score, the better a helmet performed in testing.

Then, to each helmet it tests, Virginia Tech awards an overall STAR rating (one through five); helmets with four- and five-STARs are “recommended.” The lab does not recommend helmets scoring three STARs or fewer.

Virginia Tech has tested and published results on more than 300 bicycle helmets. To date, the lab has awarded 56 helmets its coveted 5-STAR rating, and another 104 received 4 STARs. To make researching and choosing a new helmet easier, it also sorts the helmets it tests into mountain, road, urban, multi-sport, full-face, and E-bike categories. Of the 5-STAR helmets, 21 of them are road lids.

Editor’s Note: These helmets are the top 5-rated road bike helmets in Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet rankings as of November 9, 2026. The Virginia Tech helmet lab regularly tests helmets and updates the overall rankings; the top 5 can change at any time. Please consult Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet ranking list for up-to-date rankings.

“Who is Pikio?” and “What is a Si Oblik?” Those were the questions our editors all asked when we saw this helmet rocket to the top of Virginia Tech’s STAR ratings. The Pikio isn’t only the top-rated road helmet; it’s also Virginia Tech’s best-performing helmet, period. It beats the others by a considerable margin, logging an unbelievably low 4.61 STAR score. For context, the difference between the Pikio and the second-place overall Canyon Deflectr RLS mountain bike helmet is 2.21 points; that’s the same gap between the 2nd and 28th positions in current rankings.

All of that safety comes at a relatively steep $379 cost. While the Si Oblik’s price aligns with other range-topping helmets from Giro, POC, Specialized, and MET, Pikio’s looks and finish feel comparable to mid-tier models from more well-known brands. For example, Pikio’s color options are somewhat conservative choices, and the rear strap anchor point is through-shell.

The Si Oblik fits well and has a broad range of adjustment for my medium-sized head. The rear adjusts up and down (to account for head shape and hairstyles) and features a dial to microadjust fit. The straps, however, are not as cleanly executed as expected for the price, especially compared to POC or Specialized, and I found them slightly tedious to adjust. On road and gravel rides, the Si Oblik’s airflow doesn’t feel bad, but I didn’t test this lid in peak summer heat. And while the Pikio weighs about the same as Giro and MET helmets in this test, it feels physically bigger, though not as mushroomy as the POC Cytal.

For a new brand, Pikio Labs made a solid first effort. Unlike its competitors, Pikio doesn’t have decades of trial and error or a flashy WorldTour team. Hopefully, as the company grows, it can dial in details, sharpen pricing, and spice up the aesthetic, because the Si Oblik already sets a very high bar for safety.

The POC Cytal’s unique shape and bold look make it easy to spot in a peloton. Another reason the Cytal stands out is due to its overall size—it’s a physically big lid. But despite its dimensions and slightly heavy weight, it doesn’t feel that large on your head while riding and ventilates surprisingly well.

The Cytal’s great ventilation comes from its massive vents and internal air channels that funnel air directly over your forehead while riding. I found out how well it vents while riding over the summer in France during “la canicule” (the heatwave). I could still feel the Cytal pushing air in 100-degree temps, even if it was roasting hot.

In our recent review of P2R’s $100 aero-helmet, ride tester Tom Messina said it “has no business being this good.” And with its lower price and STAR score, we say the same thing about P2R’s $60 A20 Mips. With its excellent safety rating, great adjustability, and budget-friendly price, the A20 Mips outperforms many helmets that cost three, four, or even five times its price.

P2R somehow hits the A20’s low price without cutting corners on features. It has nice straps with adjustable quick clamps that offer plenty of adjustment. P2R also includes a USB-rechargeable light that magnetically clips into the rear vent for commuting or extra visibility on the road.

The one downside we found with the A20 Mips is that it feels optimized for rounder head shapes. While it fits me well, a couple of others who tried it on said it was a little snug near their temples.

Given the Trenta 3K Carbon’s pedigree, it’s hard not to name it “Best for Racing.” UAE Team Emirates’ official sponsor is MET, and the Trenta is one of the helmets it supplies to the squad—including Tour de France champion Tadej Pogačar and World Champion Brandon McNulty. While UAE riders often race the Italian brand’s Manta aero helmet, they sometimes pick the lightweight, well-ventilated Trenta 3K Carbon for climbing stages and training.

Unlike some modern helmets with similarly strong protection, the Trenta feels light and racey on your head, and almost disappears when you’re riding. The straps offer good adjustability, and the Mips Air Node liner protects without feeling bulky. However, the Trenta’s biggest drawback is its price tag. At over $500, this is an expensive piece of kit.

Ranked 14th overall and 5th in road helmets, Giro’s Aries Spherical stands out in our testing for its overall comfort, adjustability, low weight, and great looks. While its STAR score is much higher than the first-place Pikio, the Aries is a very safe helmet and received Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR rating. Having crashed on the road while wearing an Aries Spherical, I also know this helmet works.

Of the approximately one dozen road and gravel helmets in my rotation at any given time, I reach for the Aries Spherical most often. The Aries fits my head perfectly, and the Roc Loc dial system offers plenty of adjustability for hair length or if I’m wearing a cap underneath in rain or cold weather. Giro makes the Aries in a wide range of colors and graphics to fit almost any rider’s personality or fashion.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8890. 6 Tips for Maintaining Your Fitness Routine During the Busy Holiday Season

Use these strategies to keep your training on track so you can start the new year feeling strong.

The holiday season has arrived, and with it, plenty of reasons your fitness routine may slide. Between shopping for gifts, attending holiday parties, and meeting work obligations, it can feel like there’s not enough time to squeeze in an hour-long workout session—so why even try?

Well, consider this: You don’t have to do as much as you think to maintain your fitness between now and New Year’s Day. A review published in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research in 2021 suggests that you can reduce your workout time by two-thirds and still maintain your gains, as long as the intensity stays the same.

Researchers also found that, in generally active adults, cutting training frequency to just twice a week for up to 15 weeks could maintain short-term endurance and VO₂ max.

Setting an attainable goal for yourself, like running for at least 30 minutes two or three times per week, can make staying active through the holidays feel more doable. It’s how I was able to get back to exercise after a break, and it’s also how I plan to maintain my fitness this winter—in addition to following some of the best advice from my Runner’s World colleagues.

So ditch the all-or-nothing mindset and use the following tips to your advantage now, so when the New Year arrives, you’ll be ready to tackle your goals for 2027.

“I have a race in mid-January, so I am following a training plan [which keeps me motivated]. But I am also cross-training with step aerobics, and I’ve added jump training into my workouts. I was bored with my usual strength routine, so I decided to mix things up with kettlebell training, targeting my upper body and core.” —Donna Raskin, senior health and fitness editor

“I make time for new workout classes, like the ones offered by Solidcore and OrangeTheory to support my strength needs, because I usually don’t get to attend those sessions when I’m training for a race.” —Sara Hemstock, senior director of marketing and brand liaison

“I love doing strength work and some form of speed training in the winter. I recently found an indoor track in my local YMCA, and I’m excited to use that as an option for when it snows. There’s something nostalgic about it for me after running winter track as a kid.” —Kristine Kearns, associate health and fitness editor

“I love running on Christmas Day because it’s always so quiet in my hometown of Columbia, South Carolina. I usually run downtown, past the state capitol building, and through the University of South Carolina. The normally busy area turns into a complete ghost town! It’s a once-a-year experience and a personal tradition. I look forward to it every year.” —Theo Khaler, news editor

“Every year, I look forward to going home to North Carolina during the holidays because I get to test my fitness in my neighborhood Turkey Trot. It’s a community event put on by my high school, and it always draws a huge crowd.

The 5K race itself gives me something to look toward and train for in the fall. It’s a great chance to test my speed and have fun with the sport, but the best part has to be the community aspect. I catch up with old friends, teammates, coaches, teachers, and neighbors, and hearing about their own running journeys always fuels mine, too. Plus, each age-group winner wins a pie. Who doesn’t like free dessert?” —Ashley Tysiac, content hype editor

“I motivate myself by thinking of all the folks who decided not to run as I was bundled up, gutting out a sub-freezing effort. It just makes me feel proud thinking that I decided to lace up and get out the door that particular day when someone else may not have.

The thought process works both ways: If I decide to skip a cold-weather run, I think about all the people who are out there toughing it out while I’m sipping hot chocolate on my couch.” —Matt Rudisill, associate service editor

“This is the time of year when I try to add strength work into my routine because I am usually indoors at the gym more. But I find strength training so boring, so I experiment with different protein shakes to find the ones I really like, which keeps me motivated. I consider them a postworkout treat!” —Amanda Furrer, running reviews editor

“I treat myself to nice, new running clothes, and that makes cold weather running more enjoyable. I also like testing out new looks. It gives me something to look forward to.”—Hemstock

“Indoor workouts allow me to experiment with different outfits, like a shirt with comfortable sweatpants or oversized sweatsuits. That makes me feel really cozy and confident so I want to keep on training.” —Kearns

“I try to run at least a mile every day through the holidays, like a running streak. It can be inside or outside.” —Furrer

“I give myself permission to shorten any and all workouts. Even if I just commit to 20 minutes, I usually end up doing more, but knowing I can stop early breaks down the barrier to getting started.” —Mallory Creveling, deputy editor, health and fitness.

Monique LeBrun is a health and fitness editor who is based in Easton, Pennsylvania. She covers a wide range of health and wellness topics, with a primary focus on running performance and nutrition. Monique is passionate about creating content that empowers runners to become the best versions of themselves. As an avid runner and parent, she loves spending time outdoors with her daughter, who often accompanies her on weekend runs as her personal mini run coach.

The gold standard business class redemption using British Airways Avios

Picture this: you're seated in a private suite at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, your door clicked shut behind you, a glass of Dom Pérignon on the side table, and a fully flat bed dressed in Westin Heavenly bedding waiting for you. Your partner is in the suite next to yours — and when you lower the center dividing panel, you're sharing a meal in what Qatar Airways calls the "Double Bed" configuration. This is QSuites, and it is, without exaggeration, the single most celebrated business class product in the world. Now here's the number that stops the ChooseFI community cold: a cash ticket in QSuites from New York JFK to Doha DOH typically runs **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's a mortgage payment. That's a family vacation budget. That's real money that compounds in an index fund. With Qatar Avios through the Privilege Club program, that same seat costs **75,000 Avios**. When you do the math against even the conservative cash price of $5,000, you're extracting **6.7 cents per point**. Against the top-end cash price of $10,000, that's **13.3 cents per point** — in a world where most loyalty currencies are "worth" 1 cent each. This is a 6x to 13x multiplier on every point you've earned. Here's what makes this a genuine pricing inefficiency rather than just marketing: Qatar's award chart is fixed and partner-friendly, meaning the number of points required doesn't scale dynamically with cash prices the way most airline programs now do. When demand spikes and cash fares hit $10,000, your award price stays exactly 75,000 Avios. The loyalty program hasn't caught up to the revenue management engine, and that gap is your opportunity. For anyone on the path to financial independence, this is the travel rewards philosophy in its purest form: redirect real spending you're already doing onto the right cards, accumulate points as a byproduct, and convert those points into experiences that would otherwise require liquidating investments. The QSuites redemption is the pinnacle of that system — a **nearly free** business class experience that delivers more luxury per point than almost anything else in the world of travel rewards.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegant once you see it, and once you see it, you'll start recognizing similar patterns everywhere in the loyalty space.

Qatar prices its own flights in its own currency — and that currency is cheap to acquire.

Qatar Airways Privilege Club Avios are the program's native points currency. When Qatar sets award prices for its own operated flights, including QSuites, it prices them in a way that's competitive and fixed — not subject to the dynamic pricing algorithms that have made programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles increasingly unpredictable. Seventy-five thousand Avios for a transatlantic or transoceanic business class seat is a published, stable price. Qatar isn't trying to extract maximum value from every award booking; they want to keep the program attractive to drive loyalty.

The critical insight is this: you don't need to earn Qatar Avios through Qatar flights. You can transfer them directly from credit card programs you're probably already using.

Citi ThankYou Points → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — This is the fastest and cleanest route. Transfers from Citi to Qatar are instant, meaning you can search for availability, confirm the seat is bookable, and transfer in the same session without risk. For anyone holding a Citi Premier or Citi Prestige card, this is a direct pipeline to QSuites.

Capital One Miles → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — A strong secondary option. Capital One's transfer to Qatar takes 2–5 days, so you'll want to confirm availability first and ideally put the seat on a 24-hour hold if possible before initiating the transfer. Venture X and Venture card holders have access to this path.

Marriott Bonvoy Points → Qatar Avios at 3:1 — This is the least efficient path. The 3:1 ratio means you're effectively diluting your Bonvoy points, and transfers take 1–5 days. Use this only as a top-off strategy if you're a few thousand Avios short and have Bonvoy points sitting idle.

This is a huge deal that deserves its own callout. Qatar charges zero fuel surcharges on Qatar-operated award flights. This is not universal — British Airways Avios, for example, can pile on $700+ in carrier-imposed surcharges on longhaul awards. With Qatar Privilege Club, what you see is what you pay: 75,000 Avios plus the government taxes, which are typically modest.

Qatar allows stopovers in Doha and open-jaw routing on award tickets. This means you can build a trip that stops in Doha — giving you access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge, one of the world's premier airport lounges — before continuing to a final destination. The stopover rule turns a single award redemption into a multi-destination experience, a classic FI travel rewards optimization move.

This is the cardinal rule of all transfer-based award bookings: never transfer points until you've confirmed the seat exists. Go to qatarairways.com and run a search using the "Privilege Club" award booking tool. Select Business Class, enter your route (e.g., JFK to DOH), and look for QSuites availability specifically — you'll see the aircraft type and cabin configuration in the search results. QSuites is typically available on Boeing 777-300ER and A380 flights, not all Qatar aircraft, so confirm the product before you get excited.

Qatar Privilege Club opens its award booking window at 361 days in advance. QSuites availability is genuinely limited — this is a Difficulty 2/5 on the availability scale — and the best seats disappear quickly, especially for peak travel periods and popular routes like JFK–DOH. Set a calendar reminder now for exactly 361 days before your target departure date and be ready to book the moment the window opens. This single habit separates people who get QSuites awards from people who watch them disappear.

You'll need 75,000 Qatar Avios per person. Check your current balances across:

Decide your primary transfer source before you need the points. If you're using Capital One, initiate the transfer 5–7 days before you want to book to give yourself buffer time.

If you don't have a Privilege Club account, create one at qatarairways.com/privilege-club — it's free and takes minutes. Once you have your account number, you can link it as a transfer destination in your Citi, Capital One, or Marriott account.

Once you've confirmed availability and are ready to book, log into your credit card rewards portal and initiate the transfer to your Qatar Privilege Club account number. For Citi, this will post instantly. For Capital One, monitor your Avios balance over the next 2–5 days.

Return to qatarairways.com, log into your Privilege Club account, and book the award using your Avios balance. Have your passport and payment method ready for the taxes and fees. Confirm the aircraft type one final time at booking to ensure you're on a QSuites-equipped aircraft.

If you can't find two seats together, try splitting the booking into two single-seat reservations, then request to link them. Also try ±3 days on either side of your target dates — availability patterns are uneven. Calling Qatar's Privilege Club phone line (rather than booking online) occasionally surfaces inventory not shown on the website.

British Airways Avios uses a distance-based award chart rather than a flat-rate chart, which creates a pricing inefficiency on long-haul routes operated by Qatar Airways. While BA prices short-haul flights competitively, flights over 4,000 miles to Qatar and beyond land in a pricing band that dramatically undervalues the QSuites product. Qatar Airways is a oneworld alliance member, which means BA Avios can book any Qatar-operated award flight. The key insight is that you are booking through BA's system using BA's pricing, but flying on Qatar's hardware — and Qatar's business class product is in a completely different league than BA's Club World. This mismatch between the booking partner's award chart and the operating airline's product quality is exactly what makes this a sweet spot.

Let's build a real booking so the numbers stop being abstract.

The Route: New York JFK → Doha DOH on Qatar Airways, Boeing 777-300ER, QSuites Business Class.

Cash Price: A one-way QSuites ticket on this route runs roughly $5,000–$8,000 depending on timing and booking window. For a couple, you're looking at $10,000–$16,000 in cash — a number that probably makes the FI-minded reader physically uncomfortable.

Award Price: 75,000 Qatar Avios per person, one-way. Taxes and fees on Qatar-operated awards are minimal — typically under $100 — because Qatar charges no fuel surcharges. A couple flies QSuites for 150,000 Avios plus roughly $150 in taxes total.

The CPP: At the midpoint cash value of $6,500, you're getting 8.7 cents per Avios — nearly nine times what most people assume a loyalty point is worth. At $10,000, you're at 13.3 cents per point. Even at the conservative end, 6.7 cents per point makes this one of the top redemptions in the entire travel rewards ecosystem.

You arrive at JFK and access Qatar's partner lounge before departure — a preview of what's to come. Once aboard, you're shown to a fully enclosed private suite with a sliding door, direct aisle access from every seat, a large personal screen, and a seat that converts to a lie-flat bed stretching over 6 feet. The bedding is genuine Westin Heavenly quality. You and your travel companion request the Double Bed configuration — the center divider lowers, and you're sharing a full-width sleeping surface mid-flight.

Dining is a la carte, on-demand — no set meal times. The wine list is legitimate. The service is attentive without being intrusive.

If you've added a Doha stopover to your ticket, you deplane into Al Mourjan Business Lounge — a cavernous, beautifully designed space with dedicated dining, shower suites, and quiet zones. It is, consistently, one of the top-rated airport lounges on earth.

This is the experience your 75,000 points buy. No amount of economy class upgrades gets you here.

Do this: Book at the 361-day mark with precision. QSuites availability is genuinely scarce. The readers who get this redemption are the ones who treat the booking window opening like a product launch. Set two calendar alarms — one for 362 days out as a reminder, one for 361 days out as a launch signal. Have your Privilege Club account open and your credit card details ready.

Do this: Confirm the aircraft before you transfer anything. Not every Qatar flight uses QSuites. Qatar operates multiple cabin configurations on its fleet, and even the same route can have different aircraft depending on the day. Always verify the aircraft type (Boeing 777-300ER or A350 with QSuites) in the booking flow before initiating a points transfer. Booking "Business Class" on a non-QSuites aircraft is a common and painful mistake.

Do this: Use Citi ThankYou Points as your primary transfer partner. The instant transfer speed from Citi is a real operational advantage. When you find availability, you can transfer and book in a single session. With Capital One's 2–5 day transfer window, there's a risk the seat disappears before your Avios post. If your ultimate destination is beyond Doha — whether that's Asia, Africa, or the Indian subcontinent — building in a Doha layover costs nothing extra in points and gives you access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge, which is worth experiencing on its own terms.

Avoid this: Using Marriott Bonvoy as your primary transfer path. The 3:1 ratio means you need 225,000 Bonvoy points to get 75,000 Avios. Marriott points are valuable for hotel redemptions — burning them at a 3:1 ratio for airline miles is rarely optimal unless you have a massive surplus.

Avoid this: Waiting for a sale or hoping for better availability. Qatar doesn't run award sales. The award chart is fixed, and availability only decreases over time on popular routes. The readers who say "I'll book when something comes up" are the ones sharing their story about the year they almost flew QSuites.

Remember: Miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Keep your Privilege Club account active with at least one earning or redemption activity every 36 months. A single small transaction resets the clock.

#8888. Isakova and Hidalgo Win Final WTCS Races in Abu Dhabi, Jorgensen Podiums

The postponed WTCS Abu Dhabi brought the World Triathlon Championship Series, as it is currently known, to a close ahead of its transition to T50 racing within the Triathlon World Tour. The sprint-distance showdown still attracted many of the sport’s top names, with Olympic qualification points and the chance to finish the season on a high and build momentum into 2027.

The top spot on the podium was wide open in the women’s race, with the series’ undefeated champion Cassandre Beaugrand (FRA) absent. Add to the mix the shorter, sprint-distance format and hot, windy conditions set to play a factor, and it was anyone’s guess who would take it.

2025 world champion Lisa Tertsch (GER) was the big name going in, alongside Jeanne Lehair (LUX), who had been part of a sprint finish at the World Cup in Hong Kong the week before. However, Diana Isakova (RUS) was another athlete many had their eyes on after winning that sprint against Lehair and taking the World Cup win in Rome before that. American Gwen Jorgensen (USA) had shown glimmers of top form in recent races, placing fifth at WTCS Weihai and producing the second-fastest run split at the Grand Final in Pontevedra.

Into the warm, 82-degree water, three groups began to form near the front as the chop and currents made for one of the most difficult swims of the year.

Isakova and Lehair were among the first group out of the water, while Tertsch and Jorgensen exited more than 20 seconds behind. That deficit would quickly balloon to over 30 seconds early on the bike, with another group between them and the front of the race.

Halfway through the bike, the front group of nine maintained its advantage as the third group swallowed the second to form one large chase pack. On such a tight, technical course, the larger group offered little additional benefit as the smaller pack ahead steadily increased its lead.

At the end of the bike, Germany’s Laura Lindemann (GER) almost undid the work of the front, mishandling her bike after the dismount, almost causing a crash. Onto the run, a quick transition shot Isakova to the front, while around 36 seconds behind, Jorgensen and Tertsch were among the large group with significant work to do – and only 5km to do it.

By halfway, Isakova and Lehair were clear at the front, foreshadowing a repeat of the race in Hong Kong the week prior. Jorgensen remained 36 seconds behind but had gapped Tertsch and made her way into eighth place.

That momentum continued for Jorgensen as suddenly eighth place became third and she could see the leaders up ahead. Unfortunately, the gap was just too large at that point. Isakova made her move with over 200 meters to go, picking up her first WTCS win and cementing her remarkable end to the year.

Lehair finished second and reflected that her efforts on the bike may have affected her run: “I may have used too much energy, but I am super happy with second place and my third podium of the year.”

Jorgensen couldn’t believe her result, returning to the WTCS podium for the first time since 2016 at 40 years old and producing the fastest run split of the day.

“I thought I was out of this race but one of the coaches told me I was third and I couldn’t believe it,” she shared.

In the men’s race, this year’s Grand Final winner and sprint-distance specialist Matt Hauser (AUS) was wearing bib #1. With his prowess in the water, all eyes were on him in the absence of new world champion Vasco Vilaça (POR). Brazil’s Miguel Hidalgo (BRA), meanwhile, was looking to finally turn his training form into a result after some disappointing recent outings.

New Zealand’s Hayden Wilde (NZL) was the other big name on the lineup, having recently been approved to race both WTCS Abu Dhabi and Dubai T100. With the races falling within 24 hours of each other, that would not normally be allowed under World Triathlon rules. With his eyes firmly back on the Olympics, this was Wilde’s A-race for the weekend, according to New Zealand’s National Performance Manager Stephen Sheldrake.

It started with a windy, choppy swim that mostly stayed compact until the return to the beach, when two lines formed toward the shore. One group, including Hauser, made a beeline for the beach to get out of the water as soon as possible and run along the shore toward transition. That worked well for the Australian, who entered T1 with a small gap over compatriot Luke Willian (AUS).

Wilde found himself 39 seconds in arrears, with work to do alongside recent Iquique World Cup winner David Cantero del Campo (ESP). They were in a large chase group aiming to gain time on the lead group of 11, but on such a short, fast, five-lap bike course, their work was cut out for them.

Almost immediately, however, the gap was nearly cut in half, with Wilde driving the chase to within 22 seconds by the end of the first lap. The pace was so hot that the group split apart, with only a few athletes able to go with him on the technical course.

Perhaps that woke up the front group, which managed to limit its losses over the remainder of the bike and reached T2 with around nine seconds on Wilde and company. It was less than they would have hoped for against the stellar Kiwi runner, but the big question was whether the bike had stung his legs enough to hold him off. A slow transition from the 2025 winner of this race gave him even more work to do.

Onto the run, it didn’t take long for Hauser and Hidalgo to separate themselves at the front. Behind them, Wilde quickly recovered from his transition losses and moved through the rest of the front group alongside Shachar Sagiv (ISR).

The front two continued to push the pace and began adding time to Wilde behind. Hidalgo made his move before the second lap, and Hauser wasn’t able to respond. He quickly began to lose ground as the Brazilian looked comfortable all the way to the finish, taking the tape with an unmatched 14:20 5km.

It was a much-needed WTCS win to carry momentum into the 2027 Triathlon World Tour. Hauser shared afterward that he “could really feel the legs – and the whole year – in the back end of that race.”

Wilde crossed the line in third, comfortably ahead of the rest of the field, but a 14:52 5km left him short of the run speed he is accustomed to producing in these races. He won’t have much time to digest the result, however, as he immediately has to travel to Dubai, where he would look to continue his dominant T100 season.

#8887. Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

Your power meter might be working perfectly, but that doesn’t mean your cycling computer records data accurately. Here’s why you should care and how you can check.

Spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll quickly learn that they don’t always agree. Put a power meter on your crank and another on your pedals, and the numbers may not match exactly. That can be frustrating when you’re trying to figure out which one is right, but for most riders, a small, consistent difference isn’t necessarily a problem.

If you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month. Whether your threshold is actually 250 watts or 255 watts matters less than knowing that an interval at that power represents the same effort from one ride to the next.

But what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers? What if the bike computer recording your ride is changing the data before you ever upload it to Strava or TrainingPeaks?

I recently noticed something odd while testing a cycling computer. At first, I was doing this to compare GPS track accuracy, but since I was testing, I also paired all the devices to my heart rate strap and Quarq power meter. When I compared the ride files afterward, what stood out was that their power numbers didn’t match. Initially, the differences were small enough. But when I looked more closely, I noticed it immediately. Every time I stopped pedaling, one computer still recorded power.

Before I get into what the heck sticky watts are, I should say I first learned about the issue in 2025 when I saw a video from Shane Miller, who goes by GPLama on YouTube. The video is called “Power Meter Data Recording: The Wild West?”, and it’s worth watching. Shane was the first person I saw digging into this particular recording issue with cycling computers.

So what the heck is it? Sticky watts happen when a cycling computer keeps recording a power value for a few seconds after you’ve stopped pedaling. Instead of dropping to zero, the last power number gets “stuck” in your ride file until the computer finally catches up.

Let’s say you’re riding along at 250 watts and stop pedaling as you approach a corner. Your computer might continue recording 250 watts for a few seconds while you’re coasting. On a graph, that can look like a flat line extending beyond the point where the power should have dropped.

A few seconds might not sound like much, but think about how often you stop pedaling on a typical ride. Every corner, descent, stop sign, or moment spent coasting in the group is another opportunity for those extra watts to show up in your file. And if you stop pedaling after a hard effort, the computer could be holding a much higher number than 250 watts, which can skew your data.

It’s also worth distinguishing this from the setting on some computers that lets you exclude zeroes when calculating average power. That setting changes how an average is calculated. Sticky watts affect the power values recorded in the ride file itself, so those extra values can still be there when you upload the ride for analysis.

On one ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Garmin Edge 850 and an Edge 1060. The two Garmins recorded almost identical power numbers, but the DURA 2 consistently came out higher. When I looked more closely at the files, I found repeated instances where the COROS continued recording the last power value after both Garmins had dropped to zero.

The difference was especially noticeable during a series of short, hard efforts. After one effort, the DURA 2 recorded 565 watts for four seconds while both Garmins recorded zero. After another, it held 656 watts for three seconds. Across a roughly three-minute section containing several of these efforts, the Garmins averaged about 260 watts, while the COROS recorded nearly 307 watts.

Those short efforts make the issue easy to see, but the difference showed up across the ride, too. In the roughly 98 minutes of matched power data I compared, the DURA 2 averaged about 186 watts, while both Garmins averaged about 179 watts.

On a second ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Hammerhead Karoo, Wahoo ELEMNT ACE, and Garmin Edge 850. Again, the COROS recorded higher power through a section with several hard efforts followed by coasting. The Garmin recorded lower numbers than the Karoo and Wahoo in that section, which reminds us that differences can go both ways when computers record the same power meter.

I was honestly surprised to see this on the DURA 2. The original DURA had similar issues early on, but its power recording improved with subsequent updates, and it performed well in GPLama’s 2025 video presenting the issue. I don’t want to turn this into a story about picking on COROS. The company has a good history of updating and improving its products, and I expect it can address this issue on the DURA 2 as well. For now, these files show why it’s worth paying attention to what your cycling computer records, even when you trust your power meter.

If you mostly ride for fun and don’t pay much attention to your power data afterward, a few extra watts in your ride file probably won’t change your life. But if you use that data to track your training, compare rides, and work with a coach, those differences can matter.

The big problem is that sticky watts don’t necessarily add the same amount to every ride. A steady climb with little coasting might show no difference. But a ride with lots of corners, stop signs, descents, or short, hard efforts followed by coasting could produce a much larger one. That makes it harder to compare rides or judge how much work you actually did.

The easiest way to check is to record the same ride on two cycling computers paired to the same power meter. You don’t necessarily need to buy a second computer. If a friend has one you can borrow, pair both to your power meter and record a ride with a few clear transitions from pedaling to coasting.

Alternatively, you can look closely at the power files your head unit generates. Do a couple of hard efforts, like sprints, where you stop pedaling at the end, then zoom in on those sections. Look for a flat section where one computer continues recording the same power value for several seconds after the other has dropped to zero.

And yes, I know that I’m definitely in some deep weeds over here, and it can be tough to argue that a cycling computer recording a few extra watts is a huge problem worth tackling. For many riders, it might not matter at all. But the current crop of cycling computers is also the most expensive we’ve ever seen. These devices are marketed and sold as precision training tools, and accurate data recording is central to that. These devices should do that, and riders shouldn’t have to question it.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

#8886. Both Men and Women Are Quitting Running Because of Undiagnosed Pelvic Floor Problems. Experts Want to Break the Taboo So More Runners Can Get Help.

This underappreciated powerhouse is the secret to great running. But many of us don’t know how to care for it, and put up with pain, discomfort, even leakage. Here’s why it happens and what you can do about it before it derails your progress.

This article originally appeared in the Spring 2025 issue of Runner’s World.

“What fresh hell is this?” Liz B. wondered during a four-mile run on a chilly December night five months after giving birth. She was 2.7 miles into an out-and-back route when she realized she’d leaked a little urine. “It happened on and off the rest of the way home,” says the 36-year-old from central Ohio, who prefers not to use her full name when talking about urinary incontinence, which affects 25 million adult Americans.

This was not how she had envisioned her postpartum life. Liz, a physical therapist who works with stroke, brain injury, and spinal cord injury patients, had been a runner for nearly her whole life. Her father, who just ran his 91st marathon at the age of 77, had taken her out for jogs when she was a toddler, and she was hooked on long distances ever since. Her idea of a “good time” was waking up at 5 a.m. on a Saturday to go for a scenic 16-mile run with her sister. Before becoming a mom, she’d run eight marathons and was eight minutes shy of qualifying for Boston. “I had always been excited to get pregnant and had dreams of pushing my kid in a running stroller.” But her regular runs came to a screeching halt 19 weeks into her pregnancy when she developed peripheral blood clots and had to reduce physical activity because of the pain. She’d been looking forward to lacing up her running shoes again, but after a difficult labor, she developed pelvic organ prolapse, a condition where weak muscles allow one or more pelvic organs (like the uterus or bladder) to drop down onto other organs or out of the vagina.

Liz had been working with a pelvic floor therapist to treat the prolapse and had just spent the previous six weeks easing back into running. But she was frustrated with the slow progress in coming back to her pre-pregnancy eight-minute mile. “Once I had my baby, my pace slowed to a 10:30 mile,” Liz says. “And if I ran under a 9:00, I’d pee my pants a little.”

Pelvic floor dysfunction, an inability to coordinate pelvic floor muscles, is more prevalent than most of us realize. Research shows that approximately 1 in 3 women and 1 in 6 men will experience pelvic floor dysfunction in their lifetime—and that’s just what gets reported. Particularly in women, hormonal fluctuations, added weight, and the strain of pregnancy and childbirth can weaken the pelvic floor.

As much as we dislike the fact, high-impact physical activity—like running—can exacerbate these issues. That’s because as you run, your pelvic floor repeatedly absorbs impact and dampens vibrations, says Julie W. Wiebe, DPT, a physical therapist in Los Angeles who specializes in returning women to fitness after injury and pregnancy.

“Running creates an added challenge to your pelvic floor beyond the movements of everyday activities,” explains Carrie Pagliano, PT, a pelvic floor specialist based in Arlington, Virginia. “It puts greater impact and pressure on your musculoskeletal system.”

The good news is these issues can be resolved. But too often, they go undiagnosed. For one thing, there’s the stigma. Talking about pelvic floor issues can feel taboo because we’ve been conditioned to have shame around that area of the body. What’s more, most of us aren’t even sure where our pelvic floor is, what it does, or how it can become dysfunctional. But pelvic floor muscles are like any other muscles in your body. “They need training, they need relaxation, they need strengthening, and they need attention,” says Sara Reardon, DPT, WCS, a board-certified pelvic floor physical therapist in New Orleans. And finally, we need to stop accepting pelvic floor issues as normal. “When we normalize pelvic floor conditions, they don’t get treated,” says Reardon. “Pelvic floor problems are common, but not normal, and it’s the conversations about them that need to be normal.”

Here’s what you need to know to keep your pelvic floor in shape and your running on track.

Your pelvic floor consists of a group of muscles going from your pubic bone, which is located just below your abdomen, to your tailbone, which is at the bottom of your spine. It holds and protects the bladder, urethra, vagina, prostate, bowel, rectum, and anus. Were you able to “hold it” until you got to the bathroom? That’s your pelvic floor on the job. Couldn’t wait until you reached home and had to go immediately behind a tree or a parked car? Your pelvic floor may have clocked out. Got an erection? That’s in part thanks to your pelvic floor. Had a vaginal birth? Your pelvic floor was working triple overtime. Had a great orgasm? Yup, it chimes in there too.

When you think about pelvic floor issues, urinary incontinence likely comes to mind first. In one small study, approximately 46 percent of elite female endurance runners and cross-country skiers reported leaking urine when sneezing or coughing. But urinary incontinence is just one type of pelvic floor disorder—and it’s actually least likely to make a runner seek medical help. “They’re worried they’ll be told to stop running,” Pagliano says. More often, what draws runners with pelvic problems into an expert’s office are other symptoms: not being able to urinate or defecate, having sharp or nagging pelvic pain, pelvic organ prolapse, or fecal incontinence.

Despite its importance, the pelvic floor is under-researched. “The truth is we’ve never cared about pelvic health as a society,” says Wiebe. It’s been seen as a primarily women’s issue, and historically women are underrepresented in medical research. And because pelvic floor issues are mainly linked to postpartum health, men tend to be left out of the conversation as well; experts are only beginning to understand the impact it has on men.

An hour after Gordon Garner wrapped up the perfect 20-mile training run, he called his wife to let her know he was driving himself to the emergency room.

Over the previous year, the then 38-year-old software development manager had been transforming into a runner. He worked his way up from doing a Couch to 5K to prepping for his first marathon. Everything about this long run had gone according to plan: He ran at his goal pace for the upcoming 26.2 miles he wanted to complete in under four hours; he stopped every six miles to hydrate; and he felt so good, he was tempted to keep running. “Stick to the training plan,” Garner told himself, as he wrapped his last mile and headed back to his Dallas home. Before he hopped in the shower, he felt the need to pee but couldn’t. After he washed up, he tried again, and only a few drops came out. The pain was excruciating.

The ER doctors quickly ruled out kidney stones, which Garner feared were causing the pain. To empty his bladder, they had to catheterize him. “I have a pretty high pain tolerance,” says Garner, who once broke both wrists playing basketball and an elbow falling from a bike. “I was in a world of pain when they put the catheter in.” Unable to determine what was going on, the hospital discharged him.

But Garner still didn’t know what was wrong and whether it would happen again—which it did at mile 12 of the marathon he was training for. Once more, he felt the urge to pee, so he stopped at the public restroom, and nothing would come out. He kept running for six more miles before dropping out.

Ultimately, it would take two misdiagnoses, three prescriptions that didn’t resolve the issue, and several more practitioner appointments until he finally found an answer from a physical therapist. “I know exactly what’s happening to you,” Garner remembers her telling him. She explained that the muscles of Garner’s pelvic floor were continuously contracting and wouldn’t relax. The correct diagnosis was a dysfunction known as hypertonic pelvic floor.

For years, the main conversation around pelvic floor problems has focused on strengthening weakness through Kegel exercises. And yet that wasn’t the case for Garner, nor is it for many others. The pelvic floor is a complex system of muscles that needs to not only contract, squeeze, and lift, but also relax and release. “Your pelvic floor can be plenty strong but not meeting the demands that are being placed on it because it’s not behaving the way you need it to,” Wiebe says. If your pelvic floor is constantly contracting, it’s clearly strong, but it can’t perform any other function at the same time.

But the relationship is not as simple as a weak pelvic floor causing leakage or a strong one leading to retention. A 2021 meta-analysis published in Cureus Medical Journal concluded that even a strong pelvic floor can lead to urinary incontinence. In fact, some young female runners who have never given birth (a life event usually linked to incontinence) can experience urine leakage. “We also have studies showing pelvic floor activation is similar between incontinent and continent runners, so the status of the pelvic floor muscles can’t be the only cause of leakage,” says Wiebe.

Experts like Wiebe consider how your pelvic floor behaves over time—not in just one moment. “If someone doesn’t leak while doing all their regular daily activities, but then leaks at the very end of a 45-minute run, that pelvic floor is pretty strong, but it may not have the endurance for a long run,” Wiebe says. “And if that person only ran 35 or 40 minutes, they might never experience running-related incontinence. Endurance is different from strength and may better explain leaks for some.”

There is more to pelvic floors than just tightening and relaxing. “A lot of people think the pelvic floor is like a light switch: It’s either on or off,” Pagliano says. “In reality, it’s more of a dimmer switch because it has to…transition from very bright to dim or from high to low very quickly, like when we’re running.” In your body, that transition looks like your pelvic floor muscles lengthening, shortening, and working more or less to match activity demand with every foot strike.

And the pelvic floor doesn’t act in isolation. “If I have a patient whose balance is off and they don’t have the ability to navigate impact as well through their ankle, knee, and hip, then there’s more work to manage impact that gets kicked up to the pelvic floor,” says Pagliano. “I often joke that the pelvic floor is like the mom of the body. If other muscles are just like, ‘Oh, I don’t want to do that,’ then the pelvic floor has to step up and do it.”

Colleen Quigley has spent the past five years crisscrossing the globe trying to relieve a nagging source of pain that often prevented her from performing her best. “I had recurring injuries in my left foot, but a lot of the time pain would also show up in my lower back or my hip,” Quigley says. “At a certain point, I wasn’t able to train at a high level anymore.” The steeplechase specialist, NCAA champion, and current world-record holder in the 4 x 1500m relay saw more than 50 different experts, flying at one point to Germany for injections into her back.

Then one practitioner noticed a particular problem. “He muscle-tested me for things that were going on in my pelvis, then he showed me an exercise to relieve tension and tested me again,” says the 2016 Olympian. “Suddenly all the problems I tested for in my pelvis disappeared.” The exercise? A tongue stretch to relieve tightness in her jaw. “Jaw tension and pelvic floor tension have a relationship,” Wiebe says. “It’s essentially both ends of the alimentary tract.”

It was a revelation to Quigley and struck a chord with other runners. Quigley’s Instagram video demonstrating the stretch she now uses as part of her warmup routine to help relax her pelvis has gathered more than 42,000 likes. Although a single change wasn’t the solution to all of Quigley’s injuries, the jaw-pelvis connection helped resolve some symptoms that doctors couldn’t explain.

Quigley’s experience illustrates shortcomings in how diagnoses are sometimes made. Doctors and patients often focus on symptoms instead of looking for the root cause. In one study, researchers in Canada screened women who came to an orthopedic clinic for lower back and pelvic pain for pelvic floor muscle dysfunction. The study found that 95 percent of the women with lumbopelvic pain also had underlying pelvic floor dysfunction that needed to be addressed.

And Quigley’s hip pain was likely related to her pelvic issues as well. “We have deep hip stability muscles that are part of our pelvic floor,” explains Reardon. “When people start experiencing a high hamstring strain or they have a deep hip pain they feel like they just can’t get to, that can be often pelvic-floor-related.” And it doesn’t stop there. Reardon says that pain from pelvic floor dysfunction can show up in various and unexpected ways, including during bowel movements and even intercourse, which is why it’s important to find an expert with experience treating these issues (see sidebar).

Fortunately, the conversation around pelvic floor issues is evolving. “We’re starting to see patterns that might explain why you and I might have the same symptoms but maybe have different ways that we find resolutions,” says Pagliano. For runners, it might be a matter of your stride, your form, or even your breathing. “If someone holds their abdomen tight while they are running or are constantly holding their breath during normal everyday activities, we often see pelvic floor muscles that have higher tone or activity and actually don’t relax when they should. Sometimes this leads to leakage with running. Just strengthening the pelvic floor below won’t matter if those muscles are already ‘on’ and have lost the ability to contract and relax.”

As for Gordon Garner, after finally finding the right therapist, he scaled back his running for a few weeks while working on stretching and breath-control exercises. In 2023, he ran 40 miles in a 24-hour period to celebrate his 40th birthday. “I was a little worried, just because I was testing these new boundaries, but with my exercises and my breathing techniques, I had no issues. I’m very in touch with my pelvic floor muscles now.”

Liz finally found a therapist who helped her establish a strength-training routine in order to coordinate pelvic floor muscles again, pay attention to her body’s signals, and get back to running. Twenty months after giving birth, she raced her ninth marathon, without having to worry about leaking midrun. When your pelvic floor isn’t functioning as it should, “you realize that everything you do—breathing, talking, laughing, moving, carrying things—everything involves the pelvic floor,” Liz says.

With the right help and a better understanding of your body, pelvic floor problems can be solved. It’s a commitment, but your running will thank you. “Clients will always say, ‘Do I have to do these exercises forever?’” says Reardon. “I tell them, ‘Yes, to some extent, if you’re going to keep running.’”

Lauren Garges, DPT, director of pelvic rehab with St. Luke’s University Health Network in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, shares a simple at-home test that can help determine if you’re suffering from an overactive pelvic floor:

• Sit on a large stability ball or a rolled-up hand towel. There should be pressure on the perineum, the space between the genitals and anus.

• Using the muscles you would use to stop the flow of urine or gas, imagine you’re trying to vacuum up a marble. Then, actively try to relax those muscles to see if they go back down, like an elevator.

“If they’re too tight, nothing may happen because your muscles are already as tight as they can get,” she says. “Or you might be able to squeeze upward but cannot feel the downward [release]. That’s a sign of tension.”

If you find contracting the muscles challenging, Garges says, it’s a sign of pelvic floor weakness.

Before you start doing kegels—especially if you have incontinence or other pelvic floor problems—see a pelvic floor therapist to ensure it makes sense to add them to your routine, as they’re not for everyone, says Nora Arnold, DPT, a pelvic health physical therapist with Johns Hopkins Medicine in Baltimore. If you get the go-ahead, Arnold offers these cues for correct form:

• It’s best to get the hang of it lying down and then progressing to adding in practice sitting and standing.

• Squeeze your pelvic floor like you’re holding back from passing gas.

• Contract as if you’re stopping the flow of urine (but don’t do this while you’re actually peeing, as it could result in bladder infection).

• Draw your pubic bone and tailbone toward one another.

• Contract as if you are drawing your sit bones together.

• Pull your pelvic floor up as if lifting your bladder toward your heart.

• You need to both squeeze and lift—people forget that second part. Make sure to fully relax the pelvic floor muscles between reps. Breathe through each contraction and relaxation.

• The number of repetitions is best decided by a PT; however, a good place to start is 3x10 contractions, holding for 10 seconds while breathing.

This deep breathing trains coordination between the pelvic floor and the diaphragm. When your diaphragm engages fully, it encourages your pelvic floor to relax and lengthen, Arnold says.

• To start, lie on your back. You can also do this in child’s pose, happy baby pose, a deep squat, or reclined sitting.

• Breathe in through your nose for four counts. Let your breath be as slow and full as possible. Your pelvic floor should relax and lengthen passively, just like your belly.

• Exhale through your mouth for six counts.

• For maximum benefit, try to incorporate this into your routine for five to 10 minutes a day. But even just 10 repetitions can make a difference.

Check experience / “As a runner, one of the most valuable things you can do is look for a pelvic floor therapist who knows sports medicine and pelvic health,” says Julie W. Wiebe, DPT. If you’re postpartum, you might also seek out someone who has worked with moms; and if you’re male, you might look for a therapist who has experience with male clients. You can find a list of providers through the American Physical Therapy Association. Read online reviews to see what other patient experiences were like.

Consider a virtual visit / While some therapy sessions may need to be done in person, many can be done remotely. If there isn’t a great pelvic floor specialist in your area, try working with a therapist online. “I’ve been doing telehealth since before COVID-19,” says Carrie Pagliano, PT. “If I can get a really good sense of why you’re having symptoms by the questions that I ask, you can get resolution. The key is getting the right ‘why.’ After that, the ‘how’ is easy.” Make sure to offer details about whether you were a bedwetter as a child, your birthing history, or when you experience pelvic floor problems, for example.

Don’t stop until you find the right one / Garner, Quigley, and Liz all had to reach out to multiple practitioners before they found the right person. “You don’t try on one pair of pants, say they didn’t fit, and then never wear pants again,” says Reardon. “You have to keep trying different medical professionals until you find the right one.”

As the former health director at Family Circle magazine, Lynya developed content to improve the well-being of its 18 million readers. She’s worked as an editor at Glamour, Essence, Seventeen, Heart & Soul, Parenting and more. She also co-edited ESSENCE’s The Black Woman’s Guide To Healthy Living. She received her B.A. in English from Harvard University, integrative health training at Duke, and plenty of life lessons in her hometown of New York City.
